newsitem.title: DUBAI: Mideast Gulf oil outlook-relief for margins distan.
newsitem.headline: Mideast Gulf oil outlook-relief for margins distan.

text.p: Gulf oil product markets will need Indian and Asian demand in February to soak up supply length and restore local refining margins to positive territory, Gulf oil traders said on Thursday.
Middle distillates and fuel oil were expected to remain well supplied despite signs of stockbuilding in Jebel Ali and run cuts at Bahrain's Sitra refinery, they said.

Gas oil was at $23.50 a barrel fob Gulf on Thursday, remaining in its $23.00-$23.50 February range and well below the current $31.00 year-high. Its premia to independent price quotes were again steady at 60-70 cents depending on sulphur content.
"It's still a miserable time (for Gulf refiners)...prices are not as high as last year and the outlook for summer demand doesn't look that great either," one trader said.
The spread to jet-kerosene narrowed sharply to $3.00 on falling Asian jet markets.

Sellers were still hopeful that a spring rally, starting with India Oil Corp's (IOC) April diesel requirements and Ceylon Petroleum Corp's March gas oil and illuminating kerosene needs, may turn round the lacklustre Gulf and Singapore markets.
IOC on Tuesday issued its tender to buy one percent sulphur diesel in April.
That was after buying a 0.5 percent cargo from Kuwait Petroleum Corp at 65 cents over MidEast quotes.
Bulls also took comfort from growing scepticism that Iraq would export refined products in the second 90-day period of the United Nations oil-for-food deal which starts March 10.
Higher product demand would help reverse negative refining margins which are depressed despite a near-nine percent in benchmark Dubai crude prices this week, traders said.
The poor state of margins in the region had prompted Bahrain Petroleum Company (BAPCO) to cut runs at its 250,000 barrels per day (bpd) Sitra plant, traders said.
Officials at the Bahrain plant were not available to confirm or give details of the alleged cut back which traders said helped tighten lengthy Gulf middle distillates markets.
"Margins last month were near record lows. They have recovered a bit with the fall (in crude prices) but are still negative," said one trader in the region.

Weaker crude prices also had Fujairah 380-cst bunker markets retreating $6 a tonne to $90. Saudi Aramco also followed the falling market reducing its A-888 bunker diesel prices as much as $11 a tonne to $206 from Red Sea ports.
